headline: Futures bounce after the worst week since April 2025, but Nvidia falls about 5% before the open after its board opened a probe into the CEO, oil fell despite the weekend strikes, and China extended its rare earth pause to Jan 10.
summary: Prices are Friday Nov 6 closes; the dashboard (prices_as_of 2026-11-06) and Massive agree. Before the open Dow futures were up about 1.2%, S&P 500 futures 0.8% and Nasdaq futures 0.8% (Yahoo, about 7:57am ET), but Nvidia traded near 176.45, down about 5.5%, after its board opened an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang over reports that he was the target of a Chinese intelligence effort. The weekend strikes on Iran did not lift oil: Brent fell 4.2% to $94.23 at 8:17am ET after Trump said new strikes were highly unlikely while talks go on (Reuters). China's commerce ministry extended its rare earth export pause to Jan 10, so Tuesday is no longer a cliff for magnets. Tuesday's CPI will have no yearly rate for the first time, because the 2025 shutdown left no October 2025 data (BLS); the monthly core number is the one to read. The put screen passes nothing, and no new swings or puts make sense before CPI and the 1pm ET 10 year auction.

signals.title: Nvidia's board opens an independent probe into its CEO; the stock falls about 5% before the open
signals.what_happened: On Sunday Nov 8 Nvidia's board said a committee of independent directors, with outside counsel, will investigate after reports that Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The board said it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised and that it has confidence in Huang (Nvidia board statement). In a memo to staff Huang admitted an affair and said he would cooperate. Reports in The New York Times and Financial Times say US intelligence agencies are concerned that the woman, Alice Huang, passed information to Beijing; she is linked to Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer accused of helping restricted Chinese firms get Nvidia chips (CNBC). Three House Republican committee chairs asked Huang to attend a closed door briefing on Nov 18 (CNBC). A company spokesperson said he will continue as CEO without interruption. NVDA closed 186.64 on Nov 6 (Massive) and traded near 176.45 before the open, down about 5.5% (Yahoo). Nvidia is about 7% of the S&P 500 (Yahoo) and reports Nov 17 (CNBC).
signals.so_what: This is a person risk, not a demand risk, but it lands on the stock that carries the whole AI trade, one week after the worst chip day since 2020. Who pays: index funds and anyone long the Nasdaq 100, because one name is about 7% of the S&P 500. Second order: Washington now has a reason to look harder at Nvidia's China sales and customers, the area most likely to bring new export rules. Third order: if the probe drags, Nvidia's Nov 17 report and the Nov 18 briefing land on the same two days, so volatility in NVDA options stays high. What would make this wrong: the board clears Huang quickly and Nov 17 shows orders still rising; then the drop is a gift, not a warning. Confidence on the facts is high; on the outcome, low.
signals.for_you: Swing: no chip setups; do not buy the gap. Puts: none on NVDA into Nov 17; rich premium here is pricing a real event. Long term: NVDA is rated 'Wait' (price falling or below support), so it stays a watch name. Watch whether other chip names hold up today: if they do, the problem is Nvidia's, not the AI trade's.

signals.title: China extends its rare earth pause to Jan 10, so Tuesday is no longer a cliff
signals.since_yesterday: Beijing acted on Monday: the commerce ministry and customs extended the suspension of the October 2025 rare earth measures to Jan 10, matching the US side.
signals.what_happened: On Monday Nov 9 China's Ministry of Commerce said in a short statement that it extends its export control waivers, due to end Nov 10, until Jan 10, as part of a broader suspension of trade countermeasures and tariffs (Reuters via ThePrint). The extension covers the October 2025 announcements, including No. 61, the rule that reached foreign made products with at least 0.1% Chinese rare earth content (Business Standard, Mining.com.au). The April 2025 licenses on seven medium and heavy rare earths, such as dysprosium and terbium, stay in place. A separate suspension of China's gallium, germanium and antimony export ban to the US is dated Nov 27; no extension of that one was found today. The US already extended its Affiliates Rule pause to Jan 10, 2027 (Federal Register, in Sunday's brief). Trump is expected to meet Xi at the APEC summit in Shenzhen later this month (Reuters); one report lists Nov 18 to 19 (Roic.ai, Sep 25). MP closed 35.41 and USAR 8.225 on Nov 6 (Massive).
signals.so_what: The most likely outcome happened, so the big tail risk for car, defense and electronics supply chains is pushed back two months, to the same Jan 10 date as the wider truce. Who loses a little: US magnet makers, whose pricing power is strongest when China squeezes. Who gains: manufacturers that buy magnets (autos, defense primes, robots). What becomes scarce is still heavy rare earths, because the April 2025 licenses never went away. What would make this wrong: a breakdown at the APEC meeting that brings the January deadline forward in people's minds.
signals.for_you: No action. MP (rated Avoid) and USAR lose the near term policy tailwind; neither is a setup. LMT is 'Buy zone now' and uses rare earth magnets; the extension removes one small risk to that verdict.

signals.title: Oil falls 4% even after weekend strikes on Iran
signals.since_yesterday: Sunday's brief expected a possible jump at the reopen; instead Brent fell 4.2% to $94.23 by 8:17am ET after Trump said new strikes were highly unlikely while talks continue.
signals.what_happened: Brent fell $4.09 (4.2%) to $94.23 at 13:17 GMT (8:17am ET) and WTI fell $3.57 (3.9%) to $87.26 (Reuters). On Sunday Trump said fresh strikes on Iran were highly unlikely while talks to end the war continue (Reuters, Fox News). Both sides reported ships hit near Hormuz, and Iran said it would answer any strike by hitting US and Israeli targets. Last week Brent fell 16% and touched a two month low of $93.22, its steepest weekly drop since the pandemic began (Reuters). Morgan Stanley said Dated Brent trades at a discount to futures, a sign of weak physical demand; JPMorgan estimated a global surplus of 1.4 million barrels a day in October (Reuters). Earlier at 5am ET Brent was $97.48 (Yahoo), so most of the drop came in US morning trading. Nov 6 closes (Massive): XOM, CVX, COP and EOG were down 9.7% to 11.5% for the week; OXY 56.38; DAL 87.20.
signals.so_what: The market now prices talks over attacks: even a weekend with strikes, a mine hit and a rocket over Riyadh could not hold oil up. That fits a market that sees a supply surplus under the war premium. Who gets paid: airlines, chemical makers and anyone who buys fuel. Who pays: producers, whose stocks already fell harder than crude. What would make this wrong: a strike that actually removes supply, like the 2019 Abqaiq attack, or talks collapsing.
signals.for_you: Swing: no energy setups; do not try to catch falling producers. Puts: none on energy. Long term: no energy name has a buy verdict. DAL is 'Accumulate on pullback' and above its zone; cheaper fuel helps it, but there is nothing to buy until it pulls back. OXY reports today; no trade into it.

signals.title: Tuesday's CPI comes without a yearly rate; read the monthly core number
signals.since_yesterday: BLS confirms it will not publish 12 month changes for headline or core CPI this month, so last week's yearly forecasts cannot be checked. Correction: September CPI was 3.7% from a year ago, not 3.5% as our Nov 7 brief said.
signals.what_happened: October CPI comes out Tuesday Nov 10 at 8:30am ET (5:30am Pacific). Because of the funding lapse from Oct 1 to Nov 12, 2025, BLS could not publish October 2025 indexes for most series, so it will not publish 12 month changes for October 2026 where the base month is missing (BLS FAQ). Headline, core, food, energy and rent yearly rates are withheld; gasoline, new car and used car yearly changes are still published (StockTitan). Monthly forecasts: RBC +0.3% headline and +0.3% core; the Cleveland Fed nowcast (Nov 6) +0.24% headline and +0.21% core (StockTitan). September was 3.7% headline and 2.6% core from a year ago (BLS via StockTitan); Kiplinger also gives 3.7%, so our Nov 7 figure of 3.5% was wrong. Treasury sells $42 billion of 10 year notes at 1pm ET Tuesday; the bond market is closed Wednesday for Veterans Day. The Fed meets Dec 8 to 9.
signals.so_what: Without a yearly headline, traders will fix on monthly core. A 0.2% core month, held for a year, is about 2.4%; a 0.3% month is about 3.7%. That is the gap between 'the Fed can wait' and 'the Fed hikes in December'. Second order: the 10 year auction four and a half hours later tests whether buyers want bonds at about 4.84% after the number, and with bonds shut Wednesday any surprise sits for a day before it can be traded again. What would make this wrong: a mixed print (soft core, hot shelter) that each side reads its own way.
signals.for_you: Swing: no entries before Tuesday afternoon. Puts: no new puts before 1pm ET Tuesday; if core prints 0.3% or more, expect premiums to rise and wait a day. Long term: a soft core number helps the rate sensitive buy zone name AEP most.

history.when: October 1 to November 12, 2025: the federal funding lapse
history.what: BLS could not collect most October 2025 prices, so it never published October 2025 indexes for most CPI series; a year later that gap means no 12 month rate for October 2026 (BLS).
history.lesson: Missing data does not remove risk, it moves it. Markets lean harder on whatever number is left, so the monthly core print can move prices more than usual.

history.what: After a weekend drone strike cut 5.7 million barrels a day of Saudi output, Brent rose 14.6% on the Monday, its biggest one day gain since at least 1988 (Reuters via The Star).
history.lesson: Oil jumps on a weekend attack only when supply is really lost. This weekend nothing was lost, and Brent fell.

source.title: The Star (Reuters): Oil jumps nearly 15% in record trading after attack on Saudi facilities (Sep 17, 2019)

cycle.differences: In 2019 the attack took barrels off the market; today flows through Hormuz are already low and the market believes in a deal, so strikes without supply loss lower risk premium instead of raising it. The 2025 data gap was a one time event, but it lands now on the last CPI before a Fed meeting that may hike.
